blocks.text: Qualitative data: nominal (named categories, no order — e.g. sex; binary if only 2 categories) and ordinal (ordered categories, but intervals between categories are not necessarily equal — e.g. mild/moderate/severe). Quantitative data: discrete (integer counts, e.g. number of fingers) and continuous (any value in a range, e.g. cholesterol level) — though in practice measuring-instrument limits mean most continuous data behave like discrete data.

Interval data has a meaningful difference between values but no true zero (e.g. temperature in °C — 20°C is not 'twice as hot' as 10°C). Ratio data adds a true, meaningful zero point, so ratios are meaningful (e.g. height, weight). In practice the interval-vs-ratio distinction is rarely important in social/medical research since most rating scales have a meaningful zero.

blocks.title: Levels of Measurement — What Each Permits

blocks.forTopic: Levels of measurement (ascending order of information content)
expansion: Nominal — named categories only, no order
Interval — equal intervals, no true zero
Ratio — equal intervals **AND** a true zero

blocks.text: Independent variable = presumed cause/predictor, controlled by the experimenter (more than one can exist per study); dependent variable = the outcome, presumed to depend on the independent variable. A mediator variable (C) explains part or all of A's effect on B statistically (via regression); a complete mediator means A cannot cause B without C, a partial mediator only reduces (not eliminates) A's effect on B when absent. By definition a mediator cannot cause the outcome B directly on its own.
**SPMM** rule of thumb: nominal and ordinal data are analysed with non-parametric tests; most measured (interval/ratio) variables are analysed with parametric tests.

facts.label: Ratio data
facts.value: true zero → ratios meaningful (e.g. height, weight)

bullets.text: Nominal = named categories, no order; ordinal = ordered but unequal intervals; discrete = integer counts; continuous = any value in a range.
A mediator (C) statistically explains part (partial) or all (complete) of A's effect on B via regression, but by definition cannot cause the outcome B directly on its own.
**SPMM** rule of thumb: nominal/ordinal data → non-parametric tests; interval/ratio data → parametric tests.

blocks.title: Measures of Central Tendency
rows: Arithmetic average; uses all data; most sensitive to outliers/skew; larger samples give a mean closer to the true population value
Antilog of the mean of log-transformed values — closer to the median than the raw arithmetic mean when the underlying log-transformed data are symmetrical
Multiplies individual values by attached weights before averaging

The 50th percentile; divides distribution into two equal halves; less influenced by extreme scores than mean but ignores most available information; suitable for nominal data treated as ordered values
Most frequent value; crude, ignores most information, can be bimodal/multimodal; most stable of the three measures against outliers

blocks.text: In a symmetric (normal) distribution mean = median = mode. In positive (right) skew, mean > median > mode (mean is pulled toward the longer tail, mode stays on the shorter side). In negative (left) skew, mean < median < mode.

In a positively skewed distribution, most **VALUES** fall to the **LEFT** of the mean (the mean itself is pulled right by a few extreme high values) — a commonly reversed detail; the 'tail', not the bulk of the data, is on the right.

blocks.title: Measures of Dispersion
rows: Sum of squared deviations from the mean / (n−1); expressed in squared units
√variance, same units as original data — the most commonly used dispersion measure
**SD**/mean (×==100%==) — allows comparison of relative spread between two differently-scaled variables (e.g. comparing variability of referral counts vs. revenue)
**SD**/√n — describes the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean, and is always smaller than the **SD**

blocks.title: Choosing a Graph Type
rows: Two continuous variables (or one, on a single axis)
Scatter diagram (two axes) / dot plot (single axis)
Box-whisker plot (rectangle spans 1st–3rd quartile with median line inside; whiskers show min/max or a chosen percentile range; outliers plotted separately; box width itself carries no meaning)

sections.title: 3. Describing Data — Normal Distribution, SEM & CLT

blocks.text: Normal distribution properties: bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean (skew = 0); mean = median = mode; kurtosis = 0 (leptokurtic = sharply peaked, high kurtosis; platykurtic/flat = low kurtosis); tails approach but never touch the x-axis. Two parameters fully specify it: mean (μ, location of peak) and **SD** (σ, spread — higher **SD** flattens the peak). Standard Normal Distribution has mean 0 and **SD** 1; a value converted to this scale is the standard normal deviate/z-score: z = (x − mean)/**SD**.

Importance of the normal distribution: (1) many statistical tests assume it; (2) mean and **SD** are independent of each other in a normal population — ==68%== of data lie within ±1 **SD**, ==95%== within ±2 **SD**, ==99%== within ±3 **SD**, irrespective of the mean's value; (3) many natural/biological measures approximate it in large samples; (4) the Central Limit Theorem: for a sufficiently large sample (rule of thumb: n≥30 for most purposes), the distribution of sample **MEANS** drawn from any population — even a non-normal one — approaches normal.

**SEM** (standard error of the mean) is the **SD** of the distribution of sample means drawn repeatedly from a population; it enables calculation of confidence intervals. Larger sample size → smaller **SEM** → the observed sample mean is closer to the true population mean, regardless of the underlying population's own variability.

bullets.text: Larger sample size → smaller **SEM** → the observed sample mean is closer to the true population mean, regardless of the underlying population's own variability.

blocks.text: Probability = frequency of an event / total number of trials; ranges strictly 0 to 1 (or 0–==100%==). If p=0 the event cannot occur; if p=1 it must occur; probability of the complementary event (not occurring) = 1−p.

Odds = frequency of an event occurring / frequency of it **NOT** occurring (a ratio of two mutually exclusive counts, not of an event to the total). Odds and probability interconvert: P = O/(1+O); O = P/(1−P).
"Odds for a ==90%== event rate" trips candidates who answer with the probability (0.9) or its complement (0.1) instead of computing odds = p/(1−p) = 0.9/0.1 = 9.

blocks.title: Probability Combination Rules
rows: Heads or tails on one coin toss; **ABO** blood groups
P(X or Y) = P(X) + P(Y) − P(X and Y)
P(male with blood group A) = P(male) × P(group A)

blocks.text: Target population = the group results should generalise to; source population/sampling frame = the accessible list from which the sample is drawn; eligible population = source population after inclusion/exclusion criteria; study entrants = those who consent/enter; study participants/completers = those who finish. Sampling error = the (measurable) difference between a sample estimate and the true population value, reduced by better sampling technique and larger sample size — distinct from bias/systematic error.

blocks.title: Random (Probability) Sampling Methods
rows: Population divided into strata, then random sample from each — ensures small subgroups are adequately represented; proportionate uses the same sampling fraction per stratum, disproportionate deliberately over-samples a small stratum
Whole pre-existing groups (e.g. **GP** practices) randomly selected and **ALL** members included — cheaper fieldwork but can reduce study power
Clusters selected randomly, **THEN** individuals randomly sub-sampled within each selected cluster — two stages of randomness, unlike cluster sampling where everyone in the chosen cluster is included

blocks.text: Non-random ('non-probability') sampling has weaker generalisability, with unknown selection probability.

blocks.title: Non-Random ('Non-Probability') Sampling Methods
rows: Stratify, then non-randomly pick a set number per stratum (e.g. first 10)
Whoever is accessible (e.g. first patients on a list)
Self-selected — may differ systematically from non-volunteers
Used for hard-to-reach groups — one participant recruits the next
All presenting patients in sequence — a form of convenience sampling
Deliberately selected to meet qualitative research objectives — includes extreme-case, critical-case, and theoretical sampling
Every nth item from a list — arguably not truly random since selection probability is influenced by list order

blocks.text: Sampling with replacement returns each selected unit to the pool before the next draw (can be picked more than once); sampling without replacement removes it (can be picked only once).

facts.label: Sampling error
facts.value: measurable gap between sample estimate and true population value — distinct from bias

bullets.text: Non-random ('non-probability') sampling has weaker generalisability, with unknown selection probability.
Sampling with replacement can re-select the same unit; sampling without replacement removes it after selection.

sections.title: 6. Inferential Statistics — Hypothesis Testing, Errors & Power

blocks.text: Science uses falsifiability (Popper), not verification: the null hypothesis (**H0**) states no difference/effect exists and is what statistical tests try to reject; the alternative hypothesis (**H1**) is accepted if **H0** is correctly rejected, and usually mirrors the research hypothesis. One-tailed **H1** specifies direction (A>B only); two-tailed specifies only that a difference exists (A≠B, either direction) — two-tailed testing halves the significance level for a given data difference, making it more rigorous and generally preferred in clinical trials, though a one-tailed test is more powerful (needs a smaller sample) when direction can be justified in advance.

blocks.title: Type 1 vs Type 2 Error & Power
rows: Incorrectly accepting a false **H0** (false negative), mostly from small sample size or large variance
Ability to detect a true difference

blocks.text: Lowering type 1 error generally raises type 2 error and vice versa.

'Power calculation' is really a sample-size calculation from chosen values of α (~0.05), power (~==80%==), the clinically relevant effect size, and an estimated variance (from a pilot or the literature). The standardised difference = (target mean difference)/**SD**; Altman's nomogram uses this plus power to read off required sample size. Ways to increase power: larger significance level (raises type 1 error risk); larger sample size; larger effect size threshold; reduce variability (precise measurement, matching); use a one-sided test if justified; use the most powerful test the data's assumptions allow.

items.text: A one-tailed (rather than two-tailed) significance test for in-utero famine exposure and schizophrenia is justified specifically because the researchers already have strong prior grounds to expect the effect runs in **ONE** direction (exposure → illness, not the reverse) — not because of sample size, distribution shape, or number of control groups, which are the tempting-but-wrong distractors.

Recruiting fewer patients than the pre-calculated sample size (175 vs. planned 300) specifically raises the chance of a **TYPE** 2 error — the chance of type 1 error is **NOT** directly tied to sample size, a distinction the 'blue rabbit' worked example in the explanation makes explicit.

The p-value does **NOT** indicate the probability that the null hypothesis is **FALSE** (a very common misstatement) — it reflects the probability of the observed (or more extreme) data occurring **IF** the null hypothesis is true. The 'not correct' statement in this **SBA** is exactly this common misreading.

blocks.text: Multiple testing inflates type 1 error — with p=0.05, testing 20 independent hypotheses on the same data yields ~1 false positive by chance alone (repeated subgroup/secondary analyses are especially at risk). Bonferroni correction: new significance level = (usual α)/(number of tests) — rigorous, prone to false negatives (over-correction), and treats every outcome as independent even when outcomes are correlated. Alternatives: family-wise error methods (Scheffé, Tukey's **HSD**, Dunnett) or false discovery rate (**FDR** — controls the expected **PROPORTION** of false positives rather than the chance of any false positive at all).

**EMI** vignette: a null **RCT** result contradicting strong prior belief/evidence after an adequately powered, rigorous 18-month trial is best labelled a **TYPE** 2 error possibility — not automatically 'the drug doesn't work' — while choosing sibling controls (who share genetic/parenting exposure with autistic probands) for a bonding study is **SELECTION** bias that would **UNDERESTIMATE**, not overestimate, the true association.

facts.label: Bonferroni correction
facts.value: new α = usual α / number of tests

bullets.text: Two-tailed tests specify only that a difference exists (more rigorous, generally preferred in clinical trials); one-tailed tests specify direction and are more powerful (smaller sample) when direction is justified in advance.
Lowering type 1 error generally raises type 2 error, and vice versa.
Ways to increase power: larger significance level, bigger sample, larger effect-size threshold, reduced variability, a justified one-sided test, or the most powerful test the data allow.

Multiple testing inflates type 1 error (~1 false positive expected testing 20 independent hypotheses at p=0.05); **FDR** controls the expected **proportion** of false positives rather than the chance of any single false positive.

sections.title: 7. Inferential Statistics — Confidence Intervals & Effect Size

blocks.text: A ==95%== **CI** is the range within which we are ==95%== confident the **TRUE** population value lies (**NOT** that ==95%== of the population falls in that range, and not that the sample mean would be reproduced ==95%== of the time). Width depends on **SE** (variability/sample size): wider = less precise. Raising the confidence level (e.g. ==95%==→==99%==) widens the interval for the same data; conversely, smaller confidence level, larger sample size, or reduced **SD** (e.g. via stratification) narrow it.

An odds ratio of 2.00 with ==95%== **CI** 1.48–2.70 (p<0.0001) does **NOT** let you estimate degree of bias, and the **CI** **DOES** show effect size (~2-fold) rather than showing nothing — 'none of the listed inferences are possible' was the correct answer precisely because every individual plausible-sounding inference offered was subtly wrong.

blocks.title: Confidence Interval — 'Value of No Difference' by Measure

blocks.text: If the **CI** of an estimate crosses the value of no difference, the result is not statistically significant. CIs inform: degree of confidence, precision, clinical significance (magnitude), and statistical significance all at once.

Effect size (**ES**) is the standardised difference in outcomes between groups, independent of sample size (unlike p-values) — the 'common currency' that lets meta-analyses combine studies using different outcome scales. Cohen's d = (**M1**−**M2**)/**SD**. An **ES** of 1 means the average experimental-group subject exceeds ~==84%== of the control group (the Common Language Effect Size, **CLES**, expresses this directly as a probability that a random experimental score exceeds a random control score).

facts.label: ES = 1 interpretation
facts.value: average experimental-group subject exceeds ~==84%== of controls

bullets.text: A ==95%== **CI** is the range within which we are ==95%== confident the **TRUE** population value lies — **NOT** that ==95%== of the population falls in that range, nor that repeat sampling reproduces the same mean ==95%== of the time.
If a **CI** crosses the value of no difference, the result is not statistically significant; **CI**s jointly convey confidence, precision, clinical significance, and statistical significance.

blocks.text: Reliability = consistency/replicability of a measure (high reliability does **NOT** guarantee validity).

blocks.title: Reliability Types
rows: Same instrument, same people, 2–14 days apart in psychiatry — long enough to avoid practice effects, short enough that the underlying state hasn't changed
Internal consistency — item-total correlations averaged; range −∞ to 1, conventional cut-off ≥0.70 for internal consistency
Correlate two halves of a scale
Continuous variables; 0=unreliable to 1=perfect; relative **ICC** is always ≥ absolute **ICC**; arbitrary bands 0.6=fair, 0.8=very good, 0.9=excellent

blocks.text: Validity = extent an instrument measures what it claims to.

blocks.title: Validity Types
rows: Expert judgement of domain coverage — not usually statistically testable
Predicts a future outcome (related concept: incremental validity — ability to explain variance **ABOVE** other existing measures)
Agrees with a **DIFFERENT** test of the **SAME** construct
Disagrees with a test of a **DIFFERENT** construct
Construct validity established via factor analysis

blocks.text: Two scales correlating highly (Spearman's r=0.8, p<0.01) does **NOT** let you conclude the shorter scale 'can replace' the longer one, or say anything about either scale's validity/reliability — a head-to-head correlation between two different instruments tests neither validity nor reliability directly, and a longer scale is not automatically superior just for being longer.

Precision (repeatability of a central value — comparable to reliability) vs. accuracy (closeness to true population value — comparable to validity); bias compromises accuracy/validity. Wider intervals and higher confidence levels both reduce precision.

Simple percent agreement overestimates true agreement because it ignores chance. Kappa = (observed agreement − chance-expected agreement) / (==100%== − chance-expected agreement). Kappa is used for nominal (categorical) agreement, weighted kappa for ordinal data, and Bland-Altman plots for continuous measures. Kappa is prevalence-dependent (very rare or very common conditions distort it — e.g. good kappa is easy for rare Capgras syndrome even with a few notable disagreements, but hard for common conditions like depression), and statistical significance cannot be tested directly from a kappa value — so raw percent agreement should still be inspected alongside kappa. Phi is an alternative measure allowing direct significance testing and small samples, but is less widely used than kappa.

items.text: "Weighted kappa is better suited than Cohen's kappa for..." ordinal data — a common trap is picking 'categorical, non-binary' data; weighted kappa specifically accounts for the **DEGREE** of disagreement, which only makes sense for **ORDERED** (ordinal) categories.

source.file: question_bank/Advanced Statstics/Choosing Statistical Tests_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Testing whether MRCPsych Paper A score correlates with Paper B score (same underlying construct — theoretical knowledge) is testing **CONVERGENT** validity, not predictive validity — predictive validity would require correlating a **CURRENT** score against a **FUTURE**, different outcome (e.g. **CASC** performance).

**EMI** worked kappa calculation trap: overall percent agreement (==70%==) is **NOT** the same as kappa (0.4) — candidates who stop at simple percent agreement without subtracting chance-expected agreement (==50%== here) will pick the wrong 'degree of agreement' answer.

blocks.text: Excluding cardiovascular disease from controls but not cases in a case-control study of reserpine and breast cancer primarily threatens **INTERNAL** validity (via selection bias in this specific study's conclusions) — not external validity/generalisability or reliability, which candidates often reach for instead.

Of several scenarios prone to regression to the mean (selecting extreme baseline **BP**/cholesterol/maths-ability scores for repeat measurement or intervention), the one **NOT** affected is a properly randomised **RCT** with a concurrent control group — because both arms regress equally, the comparison cancels the effect out. This is the 'odd one out' answer candidates often miss by assuming **ALL** repeated-measurement designs are vulnerable.

bullets.text: High reliability does **NOT** guarantee validity.
Precision (repeatability, ~reliability) vs. accuracy (closeness to the true value, ~validity); bias compromises accuracy/validity.

Simple percent agreement overestimates true agreement because it ignores chance; kappa is prevalence-dependent and its significance can't be tested directly, so raw percent agreement should still be inspected alongside it.

sections.title: 9. Reliability & Validity — Choosing a Statistical Test

blocks.text: First question: are we comparing groups on a point estimate (mean/median/proportion) — Category 1 — or testing an association/relationship — Category 2 (causal-association studies fall under Category 2)? For Category 1, then ask: (a) mean or proportion; (b) how many groups; (c) paired or unpaired/independent observations; (d) can we assume a parametric (normal) distribution?

blocks.forTopic: The 4 questions to ask before picking a statistical test
expansion: Point estimate — mean, median or proportion?
Groups — how many are being compared?

blocks.title: Choosing a Test — Category 1 (comparing a mean/median/proportion)

blocks.text: Parametric tests require: independent observations, normally distributed populations, and equal variances between populations. Assume biological variables are normally distributed unless the question states otherwise. Non-parametric tests are used when both variables are qualitative, **OR** when quantitative variables are not normally distributed; they compare **RANKS** (not just medians), so two groups can share the same mean/median yet differ on a non-parametric test.

blocks.forTopic: Assumptions required to use a parametric test (t-test/ANOVA)
expansion: Equal variances between the groups compared

blocks.title: Choosing a Test — Category 2 (testing an association)
Data Transformation Methods
rows: Best for positive/right skew; yields a lognormal curve; can also linearise a nonlinear correlation
Normalises and linearises, stabilises variance; used for Poisson-distributed counts
Linearises a sigmoid curve; used for proportions

blocks.text: Data transformation lets skewed data be analysed parametrically. CIs and geometric means can be harder to interpret after transformation.

blocks.title: Chi-Square (χ²) and Its Variants
rows: Frequency counts/proportions via a contingency table (observed vs. expected frequencies) — must be applied to raw counts, never to percentages
Replaces chi-square when >==20%== of expected cell frequencies are <5 (Cochran's criteria)
Applies if total N<100 or any cell <10
Chi-square variant testing 2 dichotomous variables' influence on one outcome
Chi-square variant using log cell-frequencies, for >2 groups/variables

blocks.text: t-tests: one-sample t-test compares an observed sample mean to a known/hypothesised population mean. Two-sample (Student's) t-test compares two group means — unpaired for independent samples (one observation per subject), paired for repeated pre/post observations on the same subjects. The t-test assumes equal variance between groups (testable via Levene's test).

**ANOVA** compares means across >2 groups via the ratio of between-group to within-group variance (F statistic); one-way **ANOVA** = 1 **IV** across >2 groups, two-way **ANOVA** = 2 IVs, repeated-measures **ANOVA** = paired/multiple-occasion data on the same subjects. **ANOVA** only tells you **SOME** group differs, not which — post-hoc tests (e.g. multiple t-tests) are needed to locate the difference. Assumptions: normal distribution within groups, equal variance across groups, independent observations (except repeated-measures).

items.text: For a 2×2 contingency table, df = (rows−1)×(columns−1) = 1×1 = 1 — **NOT** 4. Candidates who count the 4 cells directly instead of applying the formula pick 4 and are wrong.

source.file: question_bank/Advanced Statstics/Choosing Statistical Tests_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: "Which of the following is **FALSE** with regard to parametric statistics?" — the false option is 'these are best used for small sample sizes'. Parametric tests need normally-distributed data (which is harder to confirm in small samples) and are not inherently a small-sample tool; this is a straightforward-seeming **SBA** that inverts the usual framing (asking for the false statement among true ones).

source.file: question_bank/Advanced Statstics/Choosing Statistical Tests_ Attempt review.pdf

items.text: A significant two-way interaction in a 3-variable **ANOVA** means **TWO** of the three variables jointly affect the outcome — not all three, and not 'no efficacy'. Candidates conflate 'interaction present' with 'no main effect' or with all variables being implicated.

source.file: question_bank/Advanced Statstics/Choosing Statistical Tests_ Attempt review.pdf

bullets.text: Parametric tests require independent observations, normally distributed populations, and equal variances between groups; assume biological variables are normally distributed unless stated otherwise.
The t-test assumes equal variance between groups (testable via Levene's test); unpaired for independent samples, paired for repeated pre/post observations on the same subjects.
**ANOVA** only tells you **SOME** group differs, not which — post-hoc tests are needed to locate the difference.

blocks.text: Degrees of freedom = the number of values 'free to vary' once other parameters are already estimated. Estimating an unknown population **SD** from a sample loses 1 df (uses n−1, since the sample mean is already estimated). df formulas: one-sample t = n−1; two-sample t = (n1+n2)−2; chi-square = (rows−1)×(columns−1) — a plain 2×2 table has 1 df once row/column totals are fixed; one-way **ANOVA** total df = N−1, between-groups df = (number of groups−1), within-groups df = N−(number of groups).

Correlation coefficient r ranges −1 to +1 (no units); +1 = perfect positive linear association, −1 = perfect negative, 0 = no linear association. Pearson's r is for parametric (continuous, normally distributed) data; Spearman's rho (non-parametric equivalent) is used if ≥1 variable is ordinal, sample size is small, non-linearity is suspected, or distribution is non-normal — but assumes ranks are equidistant; if not, Kendall's tau is more appropriate. Correlation does not imply causation, and is not valid if no linear relationship is suspected or if observations are not independent. Swapping which variable is 'A' vs 'B' does not change r's sign or magnitude. Fisher's transformation can compare two correlation coefficients statistically. Partial correlation adjusts a bivariate correlation for a third variable.

If Pearson's r(A,B) = −0.50 and r(B,C) = +0.50, the relationship between A and C **CANNOT** be determined from this alone — correlation is not transitive. The tempting wrong answers assume A and C must be negatively correlated, independent, or 'linearly associated'.

Regression predicts one variable's value from another (correlation alone cannot do this): y = a + bx (simple linear regression), where b = regression coefficient (slope) and a = y-intercept. Correlation is a **PREREQUISITE** for regression, but correlation alone is not sufficient to justify it — the dependent variable must be continuous and (for regression) normally distributed; the independent variable need not be. The line of best fit is found by the method of least squares (minimising the summed squared vertical residuals); statisticians prefer maximum likelihood estimation for more complex regression models.

Given y (female twin weight) = 1200 + 0.4x (male twin weight), you can predict female weight from male weight but **CANNOT** reverse the equation to predict male from female — regression is directional (y is the dependent variable defined by the equation), unlike correlation which is symmetric.

R² (coefficient of determination) = proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable(s); ranges 0–1; tests goodness of fit. In multiple regression, individual R² values will not sum to more than 1. If the dependent variable is binary, logistic regression is used instead of linear regression (giving **OR**/**RR**/hazard ratios for each predictor); log-linear analysis is similar but only accepts categorical data and has no fixed **DV**/**IV** demarcation.

Logistic regression does **NOT** require normal distribution of residuals of the dependent variable (unlike **ANCOVA**, **ANOVA**, paired/unpaired t-tests) because the dependent variable is categorical/ordinal, not continuous — candidates who assume 'regression' always needs normality miss this.

source.file: question_bank/Advanced Statstics/Choosing Statistical Tests_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Multiple regression: y = a + b1x1 + b2x2 +…+ bnxn; independent variables are called covariates; two highly correlated IVs (collinearity) can distort the model. '==1 in 10==' rule of thumb: the number of variables entered should not exceed ~==10%== of the sample size (or, for logistic regression, ~==10%== of the number of **EVENTS**). Methods of building the model: stepwise (adds most-to-least significant variable — risk that statistically significant variables are not clinically meaningful); forward selection (retains a covariate if its addition changes another variable's regression coefficient, signalling confounding, regardless of its own significance); backward elimination (starts from the full model and removes covariates one by one).

facts.label: '1 in 10' rule
facts.value: variables entered ≤ ~==10%== of sample size (or events, for logistic regression)

bullets.text: Pearson's r needs parametric continuous data; Spearman's rho is the non-parametric equivalent (ordinal/non-normal/small n); correlation does not imply causation and needs a suspected linear relationship and independent observations.
Regression predicts one variable's value from another (correlation alone cannot); correlation is a prerequisite for regression but not sufficient alone to justify it.
R² = proportion of dependent-variable variance explained by the independent variable(s), ranging 0–1; individual R² values in multiple regression will not sum to more than 1.

Stepwise adds the most-to-least significant variable (risk: statistically but not clinically meaningful); forward selection retains a covariate if it changes another's coefficient (signals confounding); backward elimination starts from the full model and removes covariates one by one.

blocks.text: Multivariable analysis = one dependent, >1 independent variable; multivariate analysis = >1 dependent **AND** >1 independent variable (terms often used loosely/interchangeably).

Path analysis extends multiple regression to model 'chains of influence' among several dependent variables (e.g. A→B→C). Independent (X) variables are exogenous, dependent (Y) variables endogenous; a single-headed arrow = presumed causal path, a double-headed curved arrow = mere correlation. A recursive path model has unidirectional causal flow (no loops). Despite its older name 'causal modelling', path analysis cannot itself establish causality or prove a model correct — it can only show the data are consistent with the model.

In a path diagram, the numbers printed on the arrows are standardised **PATH** **COEFFICIENTS** (equivalent to regression coefficients), **NOT** correlation coefficients, degrees of freedom, or confidence/significance levels — a distractor-rich labelling trap.

Cluster analysis groups variables into homogeneous clusters via a similarity matrix, producing a dendrogram. Canonical correlation explores the relationship between two **SETS** of variables (via eigenvalues), e.g. risk factors vs. first-rank symptoms. Discriminant function analysis identifies which of several variables best discriminates between ≥2 groups (computationally similar to **MANOVA**).

Factor analysis identifies latent, unobserved 'factors' summarising correlations among many observed variables. Exploratory factor analysis makes no prior assumption about factor structure (uses: data reduction for >25 variables; classifying symptoms into meaningful concepts). Confirmatory factor analysis tests whether a pre-specified factor structure holds in a **NEW** dataset — used to assess questionnaire/test construct validity.

Deciding how many factors to retain: include factors until a preset proportion of variance is explained; Kaiser rule (retain factors with eigenvalue >1); scree plot (retain factors up to the 'elbow' where the eigenvalue-vs-component-number curve levels off). A factor loading ≥0.40 (arbitrary but conventional) marks a variable as making a significant contribution to that factor.

Stratification analyses a confounder's effect by splitting the sample into sub-tables/strata by confounder level, then pooling a single adjusted estimate (e.g. via the Mantel-Haenszel procedure) — useful only for **KNOWN** confounders. Standardisation (commonly for age) applies a hypothetical 'world standard population': direct standardisation applies study-sample stratum rates to the standard population; indirect standardisation applies standard-population rates to the study sample to get 'expected' rates, then compares these to 'observed' rates to derive a standardised ratio (e.g. Standardised Mortality Ratio, **SMR** = observed/expected).

bullets.text: Path analysis cannot itself establish causality — it can only show the data are consistent with the model; a recursive path model has unidirectional causal flow (no loops).

Exploratory factor analysis makes no prior assumption about factor structure (data reduction, symptom classification); confirmatory factor analysis tests whether a pre-specified structure holds in a **NEW** dataset (construct validity).

Stratification pools an adjusted estimate across confounder strata (e.g. via Mantel-Haenszel) but only works for **KNOWN** confounders; standardisation applies a hypothetical standard population (direct: study rates → standard population; indirect: standard rates → study sample, giving expected vs. observed).

sections.title: 13. EBM Framework (from the Advanced Statistics book's closing chapter)

blocks.text: **EBM** rests on 2 principles: a hierarchy of evidence guides decisions, but evidence alone never suffices — clinicians must weigh benefits/risks against patient values. The **EBM** process: define the clinical question (**PICO** — Patient, Intervention/exposure, Comparison, Outcome) → search the literature → appraise validity and results → apply to patient care.

A test's power to differentiate disease
Case-control or cohort designs (though any design can contribute)

rows: Systematic reviews, controlled trials register, methodology register

blocks.text: Even using multiple databases, only ~60–==70%== of the literature is typically covered by a search.

blocks.title: Literature Search & Reporting Bias Types
rows: Significant results go to English-language journals
Citation likelihood tracks significance and trial size
Selective reporting of some analyses, not others

blocks.title: Reporting-Standard Checklists
rows: Diagnostic accuracy studies — distinct from the **STAR*D** antidepressant trial

bullets.text: **EBM** process: define the clinical question (**PICO**) → search the literature → appraise validity/results → apply to patient care; the evidence hierarchy alone never suffices without weighing benefits/risks against patient values.

blocks.note: No Bayesian statistical framework (priors, posterior probabilities, Bayes factors as a general inferential approach beyond the specific Fagan/Bayesian nomogram for diagnostic post-test probability) appears anywhere in the three **SPMM** statistics book PDFs or the question bank explanations read for this topic. If Bayesian concepts are tested, this guide cannot support them — cross-check a general biostatistics text.

The notes describe sample-size/power calculation only conceptually (which inputs matter: alpha, power, effect size, variance) and via Altman's nomogram (a graphical read-off tool) — no explicit worked formula for computing required n from first principles appears in the source material. Verify against a statistics primer if a question requires calculating (rather than reading off or reasoning about) a sample size.

The general regression equation form (y = a + b1x1 + b2x2 + …) and the '==1 in 10==' rule of thumb are stated, but no worked example with real regression coefficients, odds ratios, or a fitted multiple/logistic regression model with actual numbers appears in the source notes. The question bank's regression items test concepts (which variable is dependent, what R² means, model-building strategies) rather than a numeric worked calculation.

The source material gives interpretive bands for **ICC** (0.6=fair, 0.8=very good, 0.9=excellent) and for kappa, and states that weighted kappa exists for ordinal data and Bland-Altman plots for continuous measures, but does not provide the calculation formula for **ICC** or weighted kappa themselves (only the plain-kappa formula is given with a worked example). If a question requires calculating **ICC** or weighted kappa by hand, this guide cannot support it from the given sources.
